source.excerpt: The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign, is the jewel of the kingdom.
trail: The line is §24 of Chapter X (Terrain) in Lionel Giles’s translation on Wikisource ↗, matching the popular wording exactly.
Suntzusaid.com ↗ reproduces the same section with Giles’s notes and the classical commentary of Ho Shih.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced Art of War section under Chapter X ↗, not among misattributed or disputed lines.
Giles’s translation was first published as Sun Tzŭ on the Art of War by Luzac & Co., London, in 1910 ↗.
source.excerptNote: Giles’s translation, Chapter X §24. The Chinese literally runs closer to “advances without seeking fame, retreats without shunning blame, whose sole care is to protect the people to the sovereign’s benefit — he is the treasure of the state.”

source.rightsNote: The underlying Chinese text is ancient and long in the public domain. The exact English wording shown is Lionel Giles’s translation, first published in 1910 — well before 1931 — so this translation is also in the public domain in the United States. Later translations (e.g. Griffith 1963, Cleary 1988) remain in copyright, but their wording differs from this one.

author.name: Sun Tzu
author.heading: About Sun Tzu
author.metaLine: trad. c. 544 – c. 496 BC · Chinese general, strategist & author of The Art of War
author.bio: Sun Tzu (Sun Wu) is the traditionally named author of The Art of War (‘Sunzi Bingfa’), the foundational Chinese treatise on strategy. Ancient tradition places him as a general in the state of Wu in the late Spring and Autumn period, though modern scholars debate his historicity and often date the text to the Warring States era (5th–4th century BC). Whoever compiled it, the work has shaped military and strategic thinking worldwide for over two millennia.

misattribution.heading: Is it really Sun Tzu?
misattribution.intro: Sun Tzu is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for fabricated “wise” quotes, so skepticism is warranted — but this one is the real thing. The only nuance is about the wording, not the source.

items.why: Unlike most feel-good lines pinned on Sun Tzu, this passage really is in The Art of War. It is Chapter X (Terrain) §24, present in the classical text and in every faithful translation ↗.

The vivid English — “coveting fame,” “fearing disgrace,” “jewel of the kingdom” — is Giles’s 1910 phrasing ↗. The Chinese speaks of protecting the people and being the “treasure of the state”; “his country” and “jewel of the kingdom” are Giles’s literary choices, so quoting this exact form is really quoting Sun Tzu via Giles.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: genuinely Sun Tzu — The Art of War, Chapter X §24 ↗ — with the celebrated wording supplied by Lionel Giles’s 1910 English translation.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The passage sits at the moral heart of Chapter X. Having spent the chapter cataloguing kinds of terrain and the general’s duty to read them, Sun Tzu turns to character: the ideal commander acts for the state, not for reputation. He will attack when advantageous and withdraw when necessary, indifferent to whether either move brings him personal glory or blame — because his loyalty is to the people and the sovereign, not his own name.
That ethic of egoless duty is why the line is quoted far beyond military circles — in leadership, business and politics — as a portrait of principled service over self-promotion.
